records.supported_name_scope: Klinaklini River is supported as representative of the selected connected river system. McClinchy Creek is a separately mapped selected tributary. Upper headstream, small/elongate lake passages and lateral tributary names remain null where not established. No single scalar name, formal registry status or precise legal naming boundary is asserted.
records.region: British Columbia, Canada; McClinchy Creek headward corridor and Klinaklini River to Knight Inlet.
records.geographic_disambiguation: The selected route is a McClinchy Creek headward/tributary route linked to the Klinaklini River, continuing through the mountain corridor and lower braiding to the Klinaklini estuary at the head of Knight Inlet. The broad lake east of the McClinchy receiving junction is not traversed by the selection. Separate component names are preserved; no uniform scalar naming is inferred.
records.completion_scope: The selected route is a McClinchy Creek headward/tributary route linked to the Klinaklini River, continuing through the mountain corridor and lower braiding to the Klinaklini estuary at the head of Knight Inlet. The broad lake east of the McClinchy receiving junction is not traversed by the selection. Separate component names are preserved; no uniform scalar naming is inferred.

naming_scope_details.source_label_disagreement: The MMA SIMBIO_HIDROGRAFIA rendered NOMBRE label places Río Zamora on the selected east–west Chilean approach that the DGA 2016 study map and IGN/INTA geography identify as Vizcachas. The same MMA view also labels the eastern Don Guillermo feeder as Río de las Chinas. These service labels are not used to override the better distinguished study/cartographic component identities. The linework remains useful for geographic correspondence; this naming discrepancy creates no unseen connector.
component_scope_limits: The representative candidate is the terminal receiving river and system identity. It does not imply that the complete 218.813 km rendered route is officially called Río Serrano.
The uppermost small tributary approach within the Ensenada de Falcón valley has no independently established separate name; its individual headwater name remains null.
Arroyo Ensenada de Falcón, Río Vizcachas, Río de las Chinas, Lago del Toro and Río Serrano refer to different components. Tributary and lake names are not inherited from the representative river.
Formal registry status remains unverified; accepted, scalar and Korean names remain null, with application false.

actual_terminal_settings_inspected: Río Serrano coastal mouth at the head of Seno Última Esperanza
supported_material_junctions: Arroyo Ensenada de Falcón and Ensenada de Flores headwater junction setting, followed by Arroyo de Bueno entering the Vizcachas corridor
Vizcachas southward valley and westward turn near Cerro Palique; Cazador tributary and international-border setting

Don Guillermo joining the lower Las Chinas corridor before the westward lake approach
Las Chinas entrance into the eastern Lago del Toro, separate Paine inflow to the northwest, and western Serrano outlet
Grey and Tyndall/Geikie feeder settings along the Serrano course before the coastal terminal
completion_scope.selected_lake_or_reservoir_passage: Lago del Toro is a natural lake passage in FID14664, between eastern Las Chinas inflow and the western Serrano outlet. The straight rendered lake segment is not treated as a river named Serrano. No selected reservoir passage is identified.
completion_scope.other_lake_settings: Lagunas del Portugués, Dulcinea and Palique lie west of the Argentine south-flowing Vizcachas reach; the selection does not serially pass through those lakes. The Paine lake chain and Grey/Tyndall lakes are tributary systems, not selected mainstem lake passages.
completion_scope.scale_limit: Original-source correspondence at generalized component/corridor scale. No exact bank, vertex, boundary demarcation, current wetness or present water-level claim.

records.region: Southern Patagonia, Argentina and Chile; Sierra Baguales/Falcón–Vizcachas–Las Chinas, Lago del Toro and Serrano to Seno Última Esperanza.
records.geographic_disambiguation: All three selected mainstem fragments are geographically accounted for. The head occupies the east-facing Sierra Baguales tributary setting along Arroyo Ensenada de Falcón, enters Río Vizcachas, follows its southward Argentine valley and westward border crossing, continues through the Baguales/Las Chinas junction setting and lower Las Chinas into Lago del Toro, crosses the lake and exits by Río Serrano to Seno Última Esperanza. Río Serrano is supported as the representative receiving-system identity, without transferring its name to the upstream rivers or lake passage.
records.supported_name_scope: Río Serrano is the terminal receiving-system representative; the Falcón, Vizcachas, Las Chinas and Lago del Toro components retain distinct names and scopes.

component_scope_limits: Do not apply Ñirehuao, Coichel, Mañihuales or Aysén to the northern land/boundary excursion.
The short northern feeder is individually unnamed in the inspected cartography; its name remains null.
Ñirehuao/Coichel, Mañihuales, Aysén and Blanco Oeste are distinct component identities; river-group membership does not make them one scalar name.

The SIMBIO hydrographic renderer places Aisen labels on part of the corridor upstream of the Simpson junction, while DGA 2004 explicitly begins Aysén at the Mañihuales–Simpson confluence. The finding retains that conflict and uses the explicit DGA segmentation for reach scope, without silently extending the map label.
The SIMBIO catalogue uses the older Picaflor/Mañiguales segmentation and Goichel/Nireguao spellings. These are bounded source variants, not formal registry verification.
Candidate, accepted/scalar and Korean names remain null; product application remains false.

completion_scope.headward_mismatch_vs_gap: The November 2012 DIRPLAN map separately depicts the international-boundary line along the eastern upland margin near La Katterfeld and the interior Ñirehuao/Coichel river. Its relief, river course and distinctive boundary shape, together with the detailed MMA hydrographic and COT land-cover views, account for the selected eastward excursion and return. The conclusion does not rest merely on absence of a hydrographic line or on the stored border flag.
actual_terminal_settings_inspected: The lower Aysén river and island/channel mouth at the southeastern head of Fiordo Aysén, near Puerto Aysén and Puerto Chacabuco; marine Pacific-connected fjord, not a lake or inland sink.
Blanco Oeste tributary joins the Aysén river upstream of Puerto Aysén.
supported_material_junctions: Northern unnamed tributary into the Ñirehuao/Coichel head reach; natural river continues south separately from the rendered border excursion.
Estero La Horqueta and the broad upper Ñirehuao/Coichel loop; Río Norte joins the selected middle Ñirehuao route.
Lower Ñirehuao joins the north-coming Mañihuales/Picaflor corridor.
Río Cañón and Río Emperador Guillermo enter the selected Mañihuales corridor.
Mañihuales–Simpson confluence and the Aysén name transition.
Lago Caro outlet into Blanco Oeste; tributary settings of the Las Rayas/Perdido corridors; Río Riesco lake-outlet connection from the west and Río Quetro from the east.
Blanco Oeste–Aysén confluence; lower Pangal/Los Palos-side drainage connection and the Puerto Aysén estuarine reach.
completion_scope.lakes_reservoirs: Lago Caro is the source/outlet setting at the southern start of the selected Blanco Oeste branch, rather than a long selected cross-lake reach. Lago Riesco lies west of that branch and contributes through Río Riesco; the selected line does not traverse Lago Riesco. Lago de los Palos is a northern lower-river-side waterbody on the DIRPLAN map, not a selected lake passage. The broader Caro feeder system includes Elizalde, Paloma, Atravesado and Azul in DGA prose, but these are not claimed as selected passages. No selected reservoir passage is identified in the acquired views; no modern exhaustive dam inventory is asserted.
completion_scope.scale_limit: Ordinary generalized component/corridor correspondence. No precise bank, vertex, international-boundary demarcation, current shoreline, continuous wetness or field-survey claim.

records.region: Aysén, Chile; northern Ñirehuao/Coichel boundary-upland excursion, Mañihuales–Aysén, and Blanco Oeste from Lago Caro.
records.naming_scope_hold_reason: Original relief/border and land-cover maps positively account for the northern terrestrial boundary excursion separately from the natural interior Ñirehuao/Coichel channel. All other selected components and the fjord terminal are covered, but no representative river name applies to the whole composite route.
records.geographic_disambiguation: All eight selected component settings are accounted for by original cartography at ordinary corridor scale. A short northern feeder and Ñirehuao/Coichel reach lead toward a rendered border/upland excursion; the mapped natural river instead remains in the interior valley. The selected return reaches the broad Ñirehuao loop and continues west into Mañihuales, then joins Simpson to form Aysén. The separate Blanco Oeste branch starts at the Lago Caro outlet setting, receives the Riesco and Quetro connections and joins Aysén. The lower river passes Puerto Aysén and ends in the southeastern head of Fiordo Aysén. The affirmatively mapped land/boundary excursion prevents a whole-object river identity; it is a completed naming-scope hold, not an unread material connector.

actual_terminal_settings_inspected: Río Seco lower cañadón and its turn toward the northwestern Laguna Dulce coastal-basin approach, with the lagoon and adjacent Atlantic shore visible together.
completion_scope.selected_lake_or_reservoir_passage: No selected reservoir or sustained lake transit is shown. The downstream line approaches Laguna Dulce; Laguna Tordillo lies north of the final reach and is not a selected mainstem passage. Mapped lower tributary/cañadón junctions remain distinct.
completion_scope.headward_mismatch_vs_gap: The whole initial plateau bend and the beginning of the mapped Río Seco approach near Ea. Inés are visible in the same original cartographic image. No additional pixels or unknown receiver are needed. A named channel is not established along the initial modeled bend; this does not prove that no ephemeral drainage can ever occur there.

records.region: Eastern Santa Cruz, Argentina; unnamed dry plateau, Río Seco/Cañadón Río Seco valley and Laguna Dulce coastal-basin approach.
records.naming_scope_hold_reason: The whole initial dry plateau bend is visible in original mapping, but no named matching natural channel is established there. The rest follows Río Seco/Cañadón Río Seco to the Laguna Dulce approach. Full geography is covered while the entire composite river identity remains unsupported.
records.geographic_disambiguation: The complete selected corridor is covered by an original IGN historical 1:250,000 map. Its principal valley is Río Seco, continuing east as Cañadón Río Seco toward Laguna Dulce. The initial modeled southward-then-eastward bend crosses an unnamed dry plateau area west of Ea. Inés, where the map does not establish one matching named natural channel. This is a completed geographic review with a name-scope hold, not an unread-source or unknown-receiver hold. The terminal setting is the Río Seco approach to the coastal Laguna Dulce basin, rather than a selected open-ocean mouth.

naming_scope_details.actual_terminal: Northwestern approach to the Laguna Dulce coastal basin
component_scope_limits: Río Seco is the supported name of the mapped main river corridor, not a scalar name for every selected position or a formal-registry determination.

Cañadón Río Seco is the printed lower-corridor form; Laguna Dulce has its own identity. Cañadón Anderson and Cañadón Porfiado are separate local drainage features, not synonyms for the selected system.
The unnamed initial plateau bend is not assigned a hydronym merely because the modeled line eventually enters the Río Seco corridor.

The map uses broken blue drainage lines and shallow-basin/lacustrine symbols. Neither those symbols nor the selected line establish uninterrupted natural flow, permanence, present water extent or discharge.

Guido and de Barrio (2004) describe Río Seco reaching the Atlantic through Laguna Dulce. That broader drainage statement does not turn the selected inland/lagoon-approach endpoint into an open-coast mouth and does not establish a permanently open lagoon outlet.
This river is not Río Deseado. The Macizo del Deseado and Complejo Río Deseado mentioned in supporting geology prose are regional/geological names, not the selected river hydronym.

reconstruction_rule: Start from the pinned r46 cumulative index and apply later append-only deltas in verified commit order, rejecting duplicate IDs. Keep base records, scope clauses, region qualifiers and assessment histories unchanged. Apply explicit status-list changes. Subtract all recorded IDs from the exact eligible initial inventory to recover unrecorded targets; pending IDs remain recorded but are not completed source reviews.
publication_boundary: Own factual name/scope findings, public official URLs, bounded geometry metadata and public continuity pins only. No original maps, crops, complete coordinates or private source/derivative/registration fingerprints. Official hosting does not establish source redistribution rights.

research_order.progress_rule: Follow the actual continental order: Americas, Asia, Africa, Europe, then other, with all rivers before lakes. Preserve original queue IDs and ranks for continuity; apply documented geographic deferrals without counting them as name research, and place deferred objects into their corrected later phase by length-descending, stable-ID order. Prior candidate and scope-held assessments remain unresolved where stated.
